Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

The real **de Rham cohomology** is $H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)=Z^k(M)/B^k(M)$, with $Z^k,B^k$ as in [[def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms]].

This is [[def-cohomology-object-of-a-cochain-complex]] in real vector spaces. Only a closed form $\omega$ represents a class $[\omega]$. For closed forms $\omega,\omega\prime$, equality $[\omega]=[\omega\prime]$ means precisely $\omega\prime-\omega=d\eta$ for some $(k-1)$-form $\eta$. Addition and real scalar multiplication are induced by those of forms. All groups on the empty manifold are zero.

external_items.statement_or_definition:
Let the laboratory region, its inertial chart and the fields and sources be those
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], with the
units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; fix the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the chart and the oriented volume form $\varepsilon$ of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]], with $\varepsilon_{0123}=+1$ and
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$.

(a) [Components] For a field pair $(E,B)$ of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, define the
covariant components of the **electromagnetic two-form** $F$ in the chart by
$F_{00}=0$, $F_{0i}:=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}:=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$
($i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$) and $F_{ab}:=-F_{ba}$, the index-raised components being
$F^{0i}=E_i/c$, $F^{i0}=-E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. Here
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the spatial permutation symbol of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]. Then $F$ is a $C^k$ type-$(0,2)$
tensor field on $U$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], alternating at every event, and the
components above are exactly its component functions: at $p\in U$ the tensor
$F(p)$ is the bilinear form $F(p)(u,w)=F_{ab}(p)u^aw^b$ on $V$ in the
coordinates $u^a,w^b$ of $u,w$ in $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. Indeed each $F_{ab}$ is
a finite sum of products of the $C^k$ functions $E_i,B_k$ of the chart
coordinates with the constants $c,\epsilon_{ijk}$, hence a $C^k$ function of
$x(p)$, and the component criterion of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]] applies.

(b) [Observer decomposition] Let $n:=e_0$ be the future unit timelike vector of
the chart and let $e_a:=F_{ab}n^b$, $b_a:=(*F)_{ab}n^b$ be the observer
components of [[thm-sr-antisymmetric-observer-decomposition]]; then
$e_i=+E_i/c$, $b_i=-B_i$ and $e_0=b_0=0$, and the invariants and square wedge
of that theorem read

$$\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2,\qquad F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=+4\,(E\cdot B)/c,\qquad F\wedge F=-2\,(E\cdot B)\,\varepsilon/c,$$

where $|\cdot|$ and $\cdot$ are the spatial Euclidean structure of the frame.
(For the same pair $(E,B)$, that theorem's optional clause (d) uses
$F_{\rm optional}^{i0}=E_i/c$ and $F_{\rm optional}^{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, so
$F_{\rm optional}=-F$ in all six components, not only the magnetic block. This
framework fixes clause (a) and uses the theorem's general algebra; its optional
SI dictionary must be converted by negating the entire tensor.)

(c) [Potentials when they exist] If $\varphi$ and $A$ are $C^1$ with
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$, and
$A^\mu:=(\varphi/c,A)$, $A_\mu:=\eta_{\mu\nu}A^\nu$, then
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$; conversely, if a $C^1$
covector field $A_\mu$ on $U$ satisfies $F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu
-\partial_\nu A_\mu$, then $E,B$ recovered from $F$ by clause (a) obey
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ with
$\varphi:=-cA_0$ and the spatial potential vector $A:=(A_1,A_2,A_3)$. Here
$\nabla$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] in the spatial coordinates,
and the spatial cross-product conventions of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] are
used. The definition does not assert that every field pair admits such a
potential; where a $C^1$ potential represents the $C^1$-or-better field of
clause (a), the field is closed in the explicit sense
$\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}=0$. This conclusion does not require second
classical derivatives of the potential: put
$H_{\lambda\mu\nu}:=\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}$, which is continuous because $F$ is $C^1$; for
every smooth compactly supported test $\psi$, substituting $F=dA$ and
integrating by parts twice, moving the derivatives first onto $\psi$
([[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]] (b)) and then off the
potential factors after commuting only the smooth test derivatives
([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]), gives $\int H\psi=0$; the
fundamental lemma (a) of [[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]]
then gives $H=0$. The framework's potential theorems establish existence only
under their stated hypotheses; [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]
supplies the coordinate derivatives $\partial_\mu$ used throughout.

(d) [Four-current and index-raising operator] With the adopted four-current
$j=(c\rho,J)$ of [[def-em-sources]], the raised-index operator $\Phi$ of
[[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]], defined pointwise on $V$ by
$\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$, satisfies
$\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$; the components of $F$
carry the tesla (T), those of $j$ carry A m$^{-2}$, and those of a
four-potential $A^\mu$ carry T m.

external_items.statement_or_definition:
Let $c>0$, let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with its restricted inertial chart, let fields and units be those of [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let the scalar-vector potential vocabulary on that region be that of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]: a **potential pair** $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^k$ on $\Omega\times I$ consists of $\varphi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $A:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^k$ jointly in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], and for a non-open time interval $I$ the joint classes in this item are read in the open-neighbourhood restriction convention of [[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]] (for open $I$ this is the ordinary class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); for $k\ge1$ the **field pair** is

$$E(\varphi,A):=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA,\qquad B(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{curl}A,$$

where $\nabla$ is the gradient, $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], and $\partial_t$ is the partial derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For $k\ge1$ the **Lorenz divergence** of the pair is $G(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$. The definitions in this item are stated on the laboratory region; the framework's fields are those of [[def-em-fields]]. No field equation is required to define the vocabulary; the existence theorem recalled in (a) has the additional hypotheses stated there.

(a) [Representations] Let $k\ge2$ be an integer and let $(E,B)$ be a field pair of class $C^{k-1}$ on $\Omega\times I$, meaning $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$ jointly as in [[def-em-fields]]. A **potential representation of class $C^k$** of $(E,B)$ is a potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^k$ on $\Omega\times I$ whose field pair is $(E,B)$, that is, $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\times I$. More generally, a potential pair of class $C^1$ represents a specified field pair whenever these two identities hold, even if the fields have greater regularity than the defining derivatives alone guarantee. This definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. When $\Omega$ is open and star-shaped, $I$ is an interval with at least two elements, and the jointly $C^r$ field data, $r\ge2$, satisfy $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, [[pthm-em-spacetime-potentials]] supplies $\varphi\in C^{r-1}$ and $A\in C^r$ in the stated restriction convention, and smooth potentials for smooth data satisfying the same equations; it does not assert a $C^r$ scalar potential for merely $C^r$ data. Equality of field pairs does not by itself assert gauge relatedness on an arbitrary region; a converse needs its own domain and regularity hypotheses.

(b) [Gauge functions and gauge equivalence] A **gauge function** of class $C^m$, $m\ge2$, on $\Omega\times I$ is a function $\chi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^m$ jointly; its **gauge transformation** sends a potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^m$ to

$$T_\chi(\varphi,A):=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi),$$

a potential pair of class $C^{m-1}$. Two potential pairs are **gauge related** when one is the gauge transform of the other by some gauge function. On pairs and generators of class $C^\infty$, $T_0$ is the identity and $T_{\chi_1}\bigl(T_{\chi_2}(\varphi,A)\bigr)=T_{\chi_1+\chi_2}(\varphi,A)$ for all $C^\infty$ generators $\chi_1,\chi_2$; hence gauge relatedness is an equivalence relation on the $C^\infty$ potential pairs, the inverse of $T_\chi$ being $T_{-\chi}$. For a fixed finite class the transform drops one order, and relatedness is used only through the transform it records.

(c) [Conditions] A potential pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\Omega\times I$ when $G(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi=0$ throughout $\Omega\times I$, and **in Coulomb gauge** in the chosen spatial chart when $\operatorname{div}A=0$ throughout $\Omega\times I$. These are properties of a pair in the stated conventions. The existence of a gauge function achieving either condition, with or without prescribed initial or boundary data, is a separate PDE conclusion with its own hypotheses and is not asserted by this definition.

(d) [Physical status] The physical content of a representation is its field pair $(E,B)$ of [[def-em-fields]]; the values of $\varphi$, of $A$ and of any gauge function are convention dependent and are auxiliary, and gauge related representations have the same field pair. The scalar potential $\varphi$ carries the volt, the vector potential $A$ carries the tesla metre, and a gauge function carries V s $=$ T m$^2$, so its time derivative and gradient have the units of $\varphi$ and $A$, respectively, consistently with [[def-em-si-conventions]]. No value of $\varphi$ or $A$ is by itself an observable or evidence for a field.

external_items.statement_or_definition:
Fix a wavevector $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and a positive angular
frequency $\omega>0$; here $k$ carries the unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\omega$
the unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$ in the SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]].
Fix complex amplitudes $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, where $e$ carries the unit
$\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $b$ the unit T of the electric and magnetic
fields of [[def-em-fields]]. Let $k\cdot x$ denote the Euclidean inner product
of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $\exp$ and $\operatorname{Re}$ be
those of the encoding definition [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]], whose
convention that physical fields are the real parts of complex expressions is
used throughout. Define, for each $t\in\mathbb R$, maps
$E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ by

$$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),$$

componentwise, and put $|k|:=\sqrt{\langle k,k\rangle}$,
$\hat k:=k/|k|$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega$. Terminology: $k$ is the **wavevector**,
$\hat k$ the **propagation direction**, $|k|$ the **wavenumber**, $\omega$ the
**angular frequency**, $T$ the **period**, $e,b$ the **complex amplitudes**,
and $\theta(x,t):=k\cdot x-\omega t$ the **phase**. Then:

(a) [Objects, domain and regularity] Both maps are of class $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, as verified below; on the whole-space laboratory region
$\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] they are an
electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]] of every finite class
$C^k$, $k\ge1$, read in the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

(b) [Phase and periodicity] At fixed $x$ the map $t\mapsto\theta(x,t)$ is
affine with derivative $-\omega<0$, so the phase decreases in time (the
$e^{-i\omega t}$ convention); $E$ and $B$ depend on $(x,t)$ only through
$\theta$ and are $T$-periodic in $t$.

(c) [Zero and nonzero waves] $(E,B)$ is the identically zero pair on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if $e=b=0$; call the wave
**nonzero** otherwise. The electric field alone determines $e$ and the
magnetic field alone determines $b$, because
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for all real $\theta$ forces $w=0$
(evaluate at $\theta=0$ and at $\theta=\pi/2$).

(d) [Status] This item fixes objects, conventions and terminology only. It
asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation, no transversality, no
energy claim and no polarization classification; those are the content of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] and [[def-em-polarization-definition]]. The
units and the propagation constant $c$ are those of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and no empirical realization or measurement is
claimed.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the phase $\theta(x,t)$ is a
real number, so $i\theta(x,t)$ is a complex number and
$\exp(i\theta(x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential
series of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; multiplying by the complex number
$e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined, so each $E_j$ and
$B_j$ is a well-defined real-valued function. Since $\omega>0$ and $k\ne0$,
$T=2\pi/\omega>0$ and $|k|>0$, so $\hat k$ is defined. The joint map
$(x,t)\mapsto(E(x,t),B(x,t))$ has the open set $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$
as its domain. For regularity, let $q=(k_1,k_2,k_3,-\omega)$ and
$y=(x_1,x_2,x_3,t)$. The exponential has derivative itself
([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), its complex
derivative is also its real total derivative
([[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]]),
and the real-linear map $\operatorname{Re}$ commutes with differentiation by
[[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]. Thus for every coordinate word
$(j_1,\ldots,j_m)$ and component $\ell$,
$\partial_{y_{j_m}}\cdots\partial_{y_{j_1}}E_\ell
=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_\ell\prod_{r=1}^m(iq_{j_r})\exp(iq\cdot y)\bigr)$,
by induction using the same chain rule; the identical formula holds with
$b_\ell$ for $B_\ell$. These expressions are continuous for every finite
word, proving the $C^\infty$ assertion in (a).
The equivalence in (c) is the elementary injectivity of
$w\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\cdot})$ on $\mathbb C^3$: if
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for every real $\theta$, then taking
$\theta=0$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=0$ and taking $\theta=\pi/2$ gives
$\operatorname{Re}(iw)=-\operatorname{Im}w=0$, so $w=0$, and the converse is
immediate. The complex notation is an encoding of real fields and of real
linear equations, not a complex physical field; the symbols $e$ and $b$ are
constant complex amplitudes, not fields. No electromagnetic equation, no
matter model and no physical interpretation is introduced by this
definition; in particular the complex amplitudes need not satisfy the
Maxwell amplitude equations, and the plane-wave expressions above are
defined for every $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$.

external_items.statement_or_definition:
Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and $\omega>0$, let $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$,
and let $(E,B)$ be the plane-wave pair of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on
the whole-space region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, with phase
$\theta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$. Suppose the amplitude conditions of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] hold, so that $k\cdot e=0$ and
$b=k\times e/\omega$. By that theorem, if the pair is nonzero then it also
satisfies the dispersion relation $|k|=\omega/c$, while the zero pair is
permitted for every $k\ne0$ and $\omega>0$, both on and off this dispersion
relation. This item classifies the polarization of that class of transverse
plane waves; it adds no field-theoretic content.

Write $e=a+id$ with the real vectors $a=\operatorname{Re}e$ and
$d=\operatorname{Im}e$ of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]],
applied componentwise in $\mathbb C^3$; since $k$ is real and $k\cdot e=0$, the
real and imaginary parts of this complex equation give
$\langle k,a\rangle=\langle k,d\rangle=0$. Put $\hat k=k/|k|$, and let
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$, $|\cdot|$ and $\times$ be the inner product, norm
and cross product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. Then:

(a) [Trace] At every fixed $x$ one has
$E(x,t)=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ with $\theta=\theta(x,t)$. The curve
$\gamma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$, $\gamma(\theta):=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$,
lies in the transverse plane
$k^\perp=\{v\in\mathbb R^3:\langle k,v\rangle=0\}$; it is the image of the unit
circle $S^1=\{(u_1,u_2)\in\mathbb R^2:u_1^2+u_2^2=1\}$ under the $\mathbb R$-linear
map $(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$; it is $2\pi$-periodic in the phase parameter
$\theta$ and satisfies $\gamma(\theta+\pi)=-\gamma(\theta)$, while the map
$t\mapsto E(x,t)$ has time period $T=2\pi/\omega$. The curve $\gamma$ is
called the **polarization trace** at $x$; it does not depend on $x$, so the
classification below is the same at every point.

(b) [Classification] Exactly one of the following three cases holds.

(i) **Linear polarization**: $\dim_{\mathbb R}\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\le1$.
When $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=1$, the trace is a nontrivial closed
segment in that span, traversed twice per period; when $a=d=0$, the trace is
the single point $\{0\}$ and $(E,B)$ is the zero wave.

(ii) **Circular polarization**: $|a|=|d|>0$ and $\langle a,d\rangle=0$. The
trace is the circle of radius $|a|$ in $k^\perp$, and $|E(x,t)|=|a|$ for all
$(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$.

(iii) **Elliptical (nondegenerate, noncircular) polarization**:
$\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=2$ and not (ii). Here a **nondegenerate ellipse centred at $0$** in a real plane $P$ means
the set $L(S^1)$ for a real-linear isomorphism $L:\mathbb R^2\to P$.
The trace is such an ellipse in $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$, and the
origin lies in the relative interior of the enclosed region
$L(\{u\in\mathbb R^2:|u|\le1\})$ in that plane. If in addition $\langle a,d\rangle=0$, the
parametrization is along principal axes and the semiaxis lengths are $|a|$ and
$|d|$; the general principal-axis computation is not asserted by this item.

(c) [Handedness] For $a,d\in k^\perp$, the cross product $a\times d$ is
orthogonal to $a$ and to $d$
([[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]), hence parallel
to $k$; define the **helicity sign**
$H:=\langle a\times d,\hat k\rangle\in\mathbb R$, whose sign is taken in the
order of [[def-real-order]]. One has $H=0$ exactly in the linear case (i), and
$H\ne0$ otherwise. This library calls the polarization **right-handed** when
$H<0$ and **left-handed** when $H>0$. Geometrically, $H<0$ means that at fixed
$x$ the electric vector rotates clockwise as seen by an observer facing the
incoming wave (looking along $-\hat k$), and $H>0$ means counterclockwise;
here the screen orientation is fixed by any positive orthonormal triad
$(u,v,\hat k)$, with $u$ to the right and $v$ up for that observer.
Equivalently, $\langle E(x,t)\times\partial_tE(x,t),\hat k\rangle=\omega H$ for
every $(x,t)$. The names "right" and "left" handedness are conventional and
both conventions occur in the literature, so later statements in this library
use only the sign of $H$.

(d) [Status] This is a classification definition. It introduces the trace,
the three cases and the sign $H$, and asserts no field equation, no
propagation, energy or empirical content. The magnetic amplitude enters only
through the two amplitude conditions $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$
recalled above; the definition covers the zero wave, both on and off the
dispersion relation, and no non-plane or non-transverse field is classified.

### Well-definedness and conventions

The real vectors $a,d$ are well defined by the componentwise real and
imaginary parts of $e$; because $k$ is real, taking real and imaginary parts of
$k\cdot e=\sum_jk_j(a_j+id_j)$ gives $\langle k,a\rangle=0$ and
$\langle k,d\rangle=0$, so $a,d\in k^\perp$ and $\gamma$ takes values in
$k^\perp$. The trace formula in (a) is Euler's formula
$\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ of [[thm-eulers-formula]] together with
the field arithmetic on the right-hand side of
$E=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((a+id)(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\bigr)
=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta)+i(a\sin\theta+d\cos\theta)\bigr)$
and the real-linearity of $\operatorname{Re}$: the real part is
$a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$, while the imaginary part is not a field. Since
$\theta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$ and $\omega>0$, at fixed $x$ the map
$t\mapsto\theta$ is a bijection onto $\mathbb R$; hence the set traced by
$E(x,t)$ as $t$ varies is the full image $\gamma(\mathbb R)$, independently of
$x$, and $\gamma$ is $2\pi$-periodic with $\gamma(\theta+\pi)=-\gamma(\theta)$
because $\cos$ and $\sin$ shift by a sign under $\theta\mapsto\theta+\pi$. The
time period is $T=2\pi/\omega$, the least positive $s$ with
$\theta(x,t+s)=\theta(x,t)-2\pi$ for all $(x,t)$; it is distinct from the
phase-parameter period $2\pi$ of $\gamma$.

For the classification, "exactly one of the three cases holds" is checked
case by case: if $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\le1$ then (i); otherwise
$\dim=2$, and either $|a|=|d|>0$ with $\langle a,d\rangle=0$, which is (ii),
or not, which is (iii). In case (i) with $\dim=1$, write $d=\lambda a$ with
$a\ne0$ (or symmetrically $a=\mu d$); then
$\gamma(\theta)=(\cos\theta-\lambda\sin\theta)a$, whose image is the segment
$\{sa:|s|\le\sqrt{1+\lambda^2}\}$ in $\mathbb R a$, traversed once in each direction between successive extrema of the scalar
factor (each such phase interval has length $\pi$). In case (ii),
expanding with the bilinearity of the inner product
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) gives
$|u_1a-u_2d|^2=u_1^2|a|^2+u_2^2|d|^2-2u_1u_2\langle a,d\rangle=|a|^2$
whenever $|a|=|d|$, $\langle a,d\rangle=0$ and $u_1^2+u_2^2=1$, so the image
of the unit circle under $(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$ is contained in the
circle of radius $|a|$ in the plane $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$; conversely,
for every $v$ in that plane with $|v|=|a|$ the coordinates
$u_1=\langle v,a\rangle/|a|^2$ and $u_2=-\langle v,d\rangle/|d|^2$ satisfy
$u_1^2+u_2^2=1$ and $u_1a-u_2d=v$, because $a/|a|$ and $d/|d|$ are orthonormal
and $v=\langle v,a/|a|\rangle(a/|a|)+\langle v,d/|d|\rangle(d/|d|)$; hence the
trace is exactly that circle. In case (iii) the vectors $a,d$
are linearly independent, so $T:(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$ is a linear
isomorphism of $\mathbb R^2$ onto the two-dimensional plane
$\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$; the image of the closed unit disk under $T$ is a
compact convex subset with nonempty interior in that plane, the image of the
open disk is its nonempty interior, and the image of the unit circle is its
boundary, so the trace is a nondegenerate ellipse centred at
$0=T(0)$ with the origin in the relative interior of that enclosed region.
The trace itself is its boundary and has empty interior in the plane. If moreover
$\langle a,d\rangle=0$, then along the principal axes $a,d$ the parametrization
$u_1a-u_2d$ has the stated axis lengths because the two summands are
orthogonal: $|u_1a-u_2d|^2=u_1^2|a|^2+u_2^2|d|^2$; no computation of
principal axes for general $a,d$ is used or claimed.

For (c), the cross product $a\times d$ is orthogonal to both factors and
alternating ([[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]), and the real Gram identity
[[thm-cross-product-norm-is-the-two-vector-gram-determinant]] says
$|a\times d|^2>0$ exactly when $a,d$ are linearly independent. Thus
$a\times d=0$ holds exactly when $a$ and $d$ are linearly dependent, that is,
in case (i); then $H=0$. Otherwise $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=2$, and
since $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\subseteq k^\perp$ are both two-dimensional,
they are equal; being orthogonal to $a$ and $d$, the vector $a\times d$ is
orthogonal to $k^\perp$, whose orthogonal complement in $\mathbb R^3$ is the
line $\mathbb R k$, so $a\times d=\mu k$ for a real $\mu$ and
$H=\mu|k|\ne0$. For the rotation identity, differentiating
$E=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ along $t$ with $\partial_t\theta=-\omega$ gives
$\partial_tE=\omega(a\sin\theta+d\cos\theta)$, so
$E\times\partial_tE
=\omega(a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta)\times(a\sin\theta+d\cos\theta)
=\omega\bigl((\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)a\times d
+\cos\theta\sin\theta(a\times a-d\times d)\bigr)=\omega\,a\times d$
by bilinearity and alternation, and taking the inner product with $\hat k$
gives the displayed identity. As a concrete check of the convention, take
$\hat k=e_3$ with the positive orthonormal screen triad $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, so
that $e_1$ points right and $e_2$ up for the observer looking along $-e_3$;
then $e=e_1-ie_2$ has $a=e_1$, $d=-e_2$,
$E(0,t)=\cos(\omega t)e_1-\sin(\omega t)e_2$ (clockwise), and
$H=\langle e_1\times(-e_2),e_3\rangle=-1<0$, consistently with the
right-handed naming. This fixes the sign convention of the cited treatment:
the source writes $E_0=\alpha-i\beta$ and calls the polarization right-handed
if and only if $\beta=\hat k\times\alpha$, which under $a=\alpha$,
$d=-\beta$ is $H=-|\alpha|^2<0$ in the circular case.

Finally, all amplitudes $e,b$ and vectors $k,a,d$ are constant and all
quantities above are computed from them by the operations of the cited items;
no limit, no integral and no field equation is used, and the definition is at
the level of classification only.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

external_items.statement_or_definition:
Retain the fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of [[def-em-fields]], the
energy density $u$ and Poynting vector $S$ of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]],
the laboratory region, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and its spatial
Euclidean structure of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], the constants and units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and the partial derivatives $\partial_j$ of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Write $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ for the
position in the spatial chart, $\delta_{ij}$ for the Kronecker symbol
($\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise), $\lvert E\rvert^2=\langle E,E\rangle$
with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and
$\times$ for the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] in the frame
basis. Let $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $\mu_0>0$ be the constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Momentum density] The **electromagnetic momentum density** is the map
$g:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ defined by

$$g:=\frac{S}{c^2}=\varepsilon_0\,E\times B,$$

in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-2}\mathrm s^{-1}$; the second equality uses
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

(b) [Maxwell stress tensor] The **Maxwell stress tensor** is the spatial
tensor field $\sigma$ on $\Omega\times I$ with components

$$\sigma_{ij}:=\varepsilon_0\Bigl(E_iE_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert E\rvert^2\Bigr)+\frac{1}{\mu_0}\Bigl(B_iB_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert B\rvert^2\Bigr),$$

in $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-2}=\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}$; the indices range over
$\{1,2,3\}$ and repeated symbols are not summed here, every sum being written
explicitly. The tensor is **symmetric**, $\sigma_{ij}=\sigma_{ji}$ for all
$i,j$, by inspection of the displayed expression. Its divergence is the vector
field with components
$(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$, the partial
derivatives being taken at fixed $t$.

(c) [Momentum flux] The **momentum flux tensor** is $\Pi:=-\sigma$, with
$(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\Pi_{ij}$; then
$\operatorname{div}\Pi=-\operatorname{div}\sigma$ componentwise.

(d) [Orbital angular momentum density and its flux] Relative to the origin of
the spatial chart, the **orbital angular momentum density** is
$\ell:=x\times g$, with components $\ell_i=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\epsilon_{ijk}x_jg_k$,
and its **flux tensor** is the spatial tensor field $x\times\Pi$ with
components

$$(x\times\Pi)_{i\ell}=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\epsilon_{ijk}\,x_j\,\Pi_{k\ell}.$$

Here $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the Levi-Civita symbol, defined by
$\epsilon_{ijk}=+1$ if $(i,j,k)$ is an even permutation of $(1,2,3)$,
$\epsilon_{ijk}=-1$ if it is an odd permutation, and $\epsilon_{ijk}=0$ if two
indices coincide, in the positively oriented basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. The object
$\ell$ carries $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-1}$ and the components
of $x\times\Pi$ carry $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm s^{-2}=\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-1}$.

(e) [Origin] Both $\ell$ and $x\times\Pi$ depend on the origin of the spatial
chart: under a shift $x\mapsto x+a$ of the origin by a constant $a\in\mathbb R^3$
their values become $\ell+a\times g$ and $x\times\Pi+a\times\Pi$ respectively,
so the definition fixes one origin in the laboratory frame and every statement
about $\ell$ or $x\times\Pi$ is relative to that fixed origin.

(f) [Status] This item fixes objects and index conventions only. No balance
identity and no interpretation of $\sigma$ or $\Pi$ as force or momentum flux
is asserted here; every balance identity involving these objects is the content
of the separate theorem items of this page.

(g) [Quadratic character and singular support] All five objects are quadratic
in the fields $E,B$. For a locally integrable branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] the exclusions recorded in
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]] apply to each of them: the products
$E_iE_j$, $B_iB_j$ and the components of $E\times B$ need not be locally
integrable, no product of distributions is defined, and the displayed formulas
then define the objects pointwise almost everywhere, the framework using them
only where the local integrability of the products is separately established.
No value is assigned at a point of singular source support.

(h) [No covariant object] No four-dimensional or covariant interpretation of
$(u,S,g,\sigma)$ is defined here; in particular $g$ is not identified with the
spatial components of a covariant momentum density.

Assume Countable Choice for weak-derivative uniqueness and the real $L^2$ product below, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open. Here $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ is the set of triples of real scalar $L^2$ classes from [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Define
$$ (u,v)_{L^2(\Omega)}:=\sum_{j=1}^3\int_\Omega u_jv_j\,dx,\qquad \|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2:=\sum_{j=1}^3\|u_j\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2. $$
Each scalar pairing is well-defined and induces its quotient norm by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]; the finite sum is therefore a real inner product on the triple space with the displayed norm. A test field $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ means a triple of real-valued members of the test-function space $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ of [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. Writing $\varphi=(\varphi_x,\varphi_y,\varphi_z)$, its classical curl is the coordinate expression of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]],
$$\operatorname{curl}\varphi=(\partial_y\varphi_z-\partial_z\varphi_y,\partial_z\varphi_x-\partial_x\varphi_z,\partial_x\varphi_y-\partial_y\varphi_x).$$
For $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, its distributional curl is the triple of scalar distributions whose action on a vector test field is the sum of the three component pairings, determined by
$$\langle \operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega u\cdot\operatorname{curl}\varphi\,dx,\qquad \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3).$$
The integral is finite because $u$ and the smooth compactly supported field $\operatorname{curl}\varphi$ are componentwise in $L^2$ and scalar Cauchy–Schwarz applies. On tests supported in a fixed compact $K\Subset\Omega$, the same estimate gives $|\langle\operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle|\le C_{u,K}\max_{|\alpha|\le1}\sup_K|D^\alpha\varphi|$ with a finite $C_{u,K}$. This proves continuity on each fixed-support test space; the LF universal property of [[lem-test-function-lf-topology-universal-property]], for the test topology of [[def-test-function-topology]], makes the pairing a vector distribution on $\Omega$.
If this vector distribution is represented by an $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ class, that class is unique almost everywhere componentwise by the injection of locally integrable functions into scalar distributions in [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], under the stated Countable Choice assumption.
Define
$$H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)=\{u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{curl}u\text{ is represented by an element of }L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)\}$$
with graph norm $\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)}^2=\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2$. No boundary condition is imposed by this definition. Fields are real-valued; equality is equality of almost-everywhere classes.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ have a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. The H(curl) and H(div) graph-space conventions used below carry their stated Countable Choice assumptions. Choose one orientation for every mesh edge and face and the ambient orientation for each tetrahedron, with incidence signs given by [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. Write $t_e$ for the unit tangent in the chosen direction of an edge $e$, and $n_F$ for the unit normal determined by the chosen orientation of a face $F$ and the ambient orientation. On a tetrahedron $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$, list the vertices in any order and let $P_1(K)$ denote scalar polynomials of total degree at most one. For an ordered edge $[i,j]$, put $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$; reversing its orientation changes the sign. Set
$$W_h^0:=\{q\in C^0(\overline\Omega):q|_K\in P_1(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The first-family lowest-order Nedelec space is
$$N_h^1:=\{u\in H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega):u|_K\in\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{ij}:0\le i<j\le3\}\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global edge }e\text{ has one common oriented circulation }\int_e u|_K\cdot t_e\,ds\text{ for all }K\supset e\}.$$
The local Raviart–Thomas space is $RT_0(K)=\{a+c x:a\in\mathbb R^3,\ c\in\mathbb R\}$. With $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$ as defined by [[def-na-hdiv-space]], set
$$N_h^2:=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};\Omega):v|_K\in RT_0(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global face }F\text{ has one common oriented flux }\int_F v|_K\cdot n_F\,dS\text{ for all }K\supset F\},\qquad N_h^3:=\{q\in L^2(\Omega):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The covariant affine Piola map for $N_h^1$ and contravariant affine Piola map for $N_h^2$ use the orientation-preserving cell maps and conventions of [[def-covariant-contravariant-piola-maps-and-hdiv-hcurl]]. Their differential and moment identities are those of [[thm-affine-piola-differential-and-trace-moment-identities]]. The edge, face, and cell degrees of freedom are respectively the oriented edge circulation, oriented face-normal flux, and cell integral.

In the two conformity conditions above, each cellwise polynomial restriction has a unique polynomial representative on its closed cell, and those representatives define the displayed edge and face integrals. Thus the global edge and face moments are part of the assembled-space definition; their correspondence with all cochains is proved by the local unisolvence and commuting-moment items, not inferred from rough-field traces.

Adopt as a modelling postulate of this framework the following constitutive branches for the material described by the macroscopic fields of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]].

**(a) [Material rest frame]** The relations below are stated in a material rest frame: an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the Minkowski model of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) in whose coordinates each modelled material element has fixed spatial position $x$, hence history $t\mapsto(ct,x)$ on the declared time interval. When this is the laboratory frame, the components below are laboratory components. Boosting the material changes both the fields and the rest observer; this postulate does not assert that the relations below hold with the same constants in every frame.

**(b) [Elementary inertial-rest branch]** In the rest frame, with constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\varepsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ (the isotropic scalar cases $\varepsilon=\varepsilon\mathbf 1$, $\mu=\mu\mathbf 1$ with $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ included), the model takes

$$D=\varepsilon E,\qquad B=\mu H,\qquad J_c=\sigma E,$$

where $\sigma\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is symmetric positive semidefinite and $J_c$ is the conduction part of the free current, $J_f=J_c+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ for a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ in $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. For a real matrix $T$, symmetric means $T^{\mathsf T}=T$, positive definite means $v^{\mathsf T}Tv>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^3$, and positive semidefinite means $v^{\mathsf T}Tv\ge0$ for every $v$. Entries of $\varepsilon,\mu,\sigma$ carry respectively $\mathrm F\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, $\mathrm H\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\mathrm S\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, where $\mathrm F=\mathrm C/\mathrm V$, $\mathrm H=\mathrm T\,\mathrm m^2/\mathrm A$ and $\mathrm S=\mathrm A/\mathrm V$; these make the three displayed relations dimensionally consistent. Local, linear and nondispersive (instantaneous) response is part of this restricted assumption. In the isotropic case an exact broadband interpretation of the constant-coefficient law additionally requires $\varepsilon\mu\ge c^{-2}$, so that the characteristic speed $1/\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu}$ does not exceed the vacuum speed $c$; without that condition, and in the anisotropic branch, the constant-coefficient law is a declared finite-band effective phase-response model and carries no universal front-speed claim.

**(c) [Causal memory branch]** Alternatively, at each fixed material position $x$, declare a bounded continuous full history $E_x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ in $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and its response $P_x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ in $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. Write $E(t)=E_x(t)$ and $P(t)=P_x(t)$ in the following formula; any field on a smaller time interval uses a declared full-history extension, not unspecified past values. The polarisation response is the causal convolution

$$P(t)=\varepsilon_0\int_0^\infty K(s)\,E(t-s)\,ds$$

for a declared real matrix kernel $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ with entries in $L^1(0,\infty)$ ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]) and units $\mathrm s^{-1}$; the integral then converges absolutely because $|K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)|\le(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}(s)|$. The convolution uses only the past history; its continuity and causality are proved in `pthm-em-causal-dispersive-response`, while passivity is an additional model condition. Spatial or temporal differentiability of the resulting fields requires separate hypotheses when used. A finitely-subtracted analytic response may instead be declared by a dimensionless scalar transfer function $\chi$ that is holomorphic on the open upper half-plane, continuous on its closure, of class $C^1$ on the real boundary away from a real subtraction point $\omega_0$, holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\omega_0$ in $\mathbb C$, and satisfies $|\chi(z)|\le C(1+|z|^{n-1})$ on $\{\operatorname{Im}z\ge0\}$ outside a compact set for some integer $n\ge1$ and constant $C>0$ ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]). Here $z,\omega_0$ are numerical angular frequencies in $\mathrm s^{-1}$ and the growth bound uses those SI numerical coordinates. Require also $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ for every real $\omega$, hence $\chi(0)\in\mathbb R$, so that the response is defined on real harmonic histories independently of their representation. For $\omega\ne0$ the amplitude at that frequency is unique and reversing frequency conjugates it; the symmetry gives the same real output. At $\omega=0$ only $\operatorname{Re}e$ determines the input, and real $\chi(0)$ makes the output depend only on that input. For $e\in\mathbb C^3$, real $\omega$, and componentwise real part, declaring this transfer means adopting the harmonic relation $E(t)=\operatorname{Re}(e e^{-i\omega t})\mapsto P(t)=\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e e^{-i\omega t})$; upper-half-plane holomorphy alone does not construct a time-domain response for arbitrary histories.

**(d) [Status]** These are adopted model assumptions, one branch at a time; the framework does not derive them from the vacuum equations or from coarse graining, and no microscopic mechanism, material data or empirical validity is claimed. Ferroelectric and ferromagnetic response, hysteresis, nonlinear response and general nonlocal response lie outside the branches declared here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]] and [[lem-em-helmholtz-boundary-representation]] ([[def-countable-choice]]); the smooth modal full-Choice branch of the latter is not used. Adopt as a model assumption of the framework the following scalar aperture-diffraction model.

**(a) [Data.]** Fix an angular frequency $\omega>0$ and wavenumber $k:=\omega/c$, with $c$ the vacuum speed of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Let $S\subset\{y\in\mathbb R^3:y_3=0\}\cap\{y:|y|\le a\}$ be a nonempty compact subset of a declared aperture plane $y_3=0$ with aperture radius $a>0$ (the screening plane and spatial region are read in the laboratory chart of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]), and let $\alpha$ be a finite complex measure on $\mathbb R^3$ supported in $S$ ([[def-complex-measure]], [[def-total-variation-of-a-signed-or-complex-measure]]) — the **aperture distribution** — with $\alpha$ read in volts so that the model field below carries the unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ of an electric-field component and its pairings are those of [[def-integration-against-a-signed-or-complex-measure]].

**(b) [Model field.]** The model assigns to every observation point $x$ with $x_3>0$ the complex scalar amplitude

$$u(x):=\int G_k(x-y)\,d\alpha(y),$$

where $G_k(z)=e^{ik|z|}/(4\pi|z|)$ for $z\ne0$ is the outgoing Helmholtz kernel of [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]], together with the real scalar field $U(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}(u(x)e^{-i\omega t})$ and the model period-averaged squared field $(1/2)|u(x)|^2$. All model predictions are declared comparisons of this squared field between observation points; no absolute radiometric power or intensity calibration is adopted.

**(c) [Adopted regime and status.]** The model is the declared polarization-insensitive scalar approximation of aperture diffraction. It ignores the vector nature and polarization of the electromagnetic field, takes the aperture distribution rather than the exact screen traces as its datum, assigns no back-reaction of the diffracted field on the illumination and no screen interaction beyond the aperture, and is not derived from either branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] or from the material-closure branches of [[post-em-material-closure]]; it is a declared optical approximation, not an exact electromagnetic model. It does not assert that $u$ or $U$ satisfies the Maxwell equations exactly, and it does not identify $\alpha$ with the unknown exact Maxwell boundary traces: assigning both $u$ and $\partial_nu$ on the aperture independently is not a well-posed exact boundary problem, as recorded in [[lem-em-helmholtz-boundary-representation]], and the error terms of [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]] are the controlled content of the model. No measured intensity, apparatus, sampling model, uncertainty budget, empirical comparison or quantitative radiometric calibration is adopted.

### Well-definedness and non-derivation notes

For fixed $x$ with $x_3>0$ and $y$ ranging over the compact support $S$ of $\alpha$, one has $|x-y|\ge x_3>0$, so $y\mapsto G_k(x-y)$ is continuous on $S$, bounded there by $1/(4\pi x_3)$; the pairing $\int G_k(x-y)\,d\alpha(y)$ is therefore the integral of a bounded continuous complex function against a finite complex measure and is defined by [[def-integration-against-a-signed-or-complex-measure]], with $|u(x)|\le\|\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}/(4\pi x_3)$ in the total variation of [[def-total-variation-of-a-signed-or-complex-measure]]. The model permits the compact closed-radius support $|y|\le a$, including aperture corners: the integral, off-support regularity and closed-radius estimates at $r\ge2a$ are established for finite measures supported in $\overline{B_a(0)}$ by [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]]. The consuming diffraction theorem also supplies direct kernel estimates at that same closed radius.

The integral against a finite complex measure, the real-field reading and the squared field $\tfrac12|u|^2$ constitute the whole mathematical content adopted here; the physical reading uses the aperture plane and spatial region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], the relation $k=\omega/c$ and the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Neither the smooth nor the weak branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] implies this scalar source model, and the finite-conductivity and material branches of [[post-em-material-closure]] contain no ideal aperture or screen model. The item uses no choice principle beyond those carried by the cited mathematical suppliers; the Countable Choice hypothesis is inherited verbatim from the kernel and boundary-representation suppliers and this postulate adds no choice use of its own. No derivation of the adopted data from the underlying postulates, and no empirical validation of the model, is claimed or implied by this item.

external_items.statement_or_definition:
Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

external_items.statement_or_definition:
Assume the memory branch of the material-closure postulate [[post-em-material-closure]] in a material rest frame, and assume the hypotheses of the mathematical suppliers [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]] and [[lem-em-finitely-subtracted-analytic-dispersion]]: Countable Choice for the smooth comparison route and, in the integrable branches, Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $E:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be the electric-field history in the material rest frame, read componentwise in its spatial basis ([[def-em-fields]]), and let $P$ be the polarisation response declared by the model.

**(a) [Causal response]** If the kernel of [[post-em-material-closure]](c) satisfies $K\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{3\times3})$, then for every bounded continuous history $E$ the response $P(t)=\varepsilon_0\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ is well defined for every $t$, bounded and continuous, linear in $E$, and causal: histories equal on $(-\infty,t_0]$ produce responses equal on $(-\infty,t_0]$.

**(b) [Transfer function and dispersion relations]** If $K$ is smooth with compact support in $(0,\infty)$, the transfer function $\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ is entire, satisfies $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ for real $\omega$, obeys $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\|K_{jk}''\|_{L^1}|z|^{-2}$ for $z\ne0$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ (with the whole-plane bound carrying the exponential factor $e^{b\max(0,-\operatorname{Im}z)}$ when $\operatorname{supp}K\subseteq(0,b)$), and its entries satisfy the principal-value dispersion relations of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]](b). If $K$ is locally absolutely continuous on $[0,\infty)$ with $K,K'\in L^1$ and $sK\in L^1$, then $\chi$ is holomorphic on the open upper half-plane, continuous with continuous first derivative on the real boundary, obeys the stated growth bound, and satisfies the same pair of relations; an instantaneous real part $\chi_\infty$ may be added to the model, and the relations apply to $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}-\chi_\infty$ for $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}=\chi_\infty+\chi$.

**(c) [Finitely-subtracted and polynomial branches]** For each specified integer $n\ge1$ for which the full hypotheses of [[lem-em-finitely-subtracted-analytic-dispersion]] hold for the declared response transfer function, its $n$-subtracted relations apply entrywise. Any transfer-only physical branch additionally requires $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ entrywise for every real $\omega$, including real $\chi(0)$, as in [[post-em-material-closure]](c); scalar transfers act as scalar matrices. These hypotheses include upper-half-plane holomorphy, continuity on the closed upper half-plane, the stated boundary $C^1$ regularity, holomorphy near the real subtraction point $\omega_0$, and the order-specific growth bound $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le C_{jk}(1+|z|^{n-1})$ outside a compact set. The Taylor polynomial and residual are

$$P_n(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{\chi^{(j)}(\omega_0)}{j!}(z-\omega_0)^j,\qquad f_n(z)=\frac{\chi(z)-P_n(z)}{(z-\omega_0)^n},$$

with removable values and the boundary $C^1$ hypothesis read entrywise as in the supplier. A growth bound for one order $n_0$ permits every order $n\ge n_0$ under the same local analytic and boundary hypotheses; it does not justify lower orders for which the required growth fails. The unsubtracted $n=0$ case is included only under its own decay and boundary hypotheses: $P_0=0$, $f_0=\chi$, growth $O(1/|z|)$, and factor $(\omega-\omega_0)^0=1$ with the supplier's principal-value convention. The separate constitutive-polynomial branch declares the normalized polarisation $P/\varepsilon_0=\sum_{j=0}^mA_jE^{(j)}+K*E$, with real scalar coefficients (acting as scalar matrices) or real $3\times3$ matrices $A_j$ whose entries carry $\mathrm s^j$, and $K$ satisfying the supplier's integrable causal hypotheses, is causal on histories with bounded continuous derivatives through order $m$. Its transfer is $Q(z)+\chi_K(z)$ with $Q(z)=\sum_{j=0}^mA_j(-iz)^j$. Subtracting the declared $Q$ leaves the proved relations for $\chi_K$, without assuming that $Q$ is the Taylor polynomial $P_n$.

**(d) [Monochromatic work, instantaneous work and passivity]** Let $\omega>0$, $e\in\mathbb C^3$ and $E(t)=\operatorname{Re}(e e^{-i\omega t})$. Write $\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)$ for the full transfer matrix used in the response: it is $\chi(\omega)$ without an instantaneous term and $\chi_\infty+\chi(\omega)$ when the arbitrary real instantaneous matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is present. For a transfer-function-only branch adopt $P(t)=\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)e e^{-i\omega t})$ as the harmonic response convention; in a kernel or normalized polynomial branch this follows by substitution. Here $e$ has units $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, $\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is dimensionless, $e^*$ denotes conjugate transpose, $(C^*)_{jk}=\overline{C_{kj}}$ for a complex matrix $C$, a matrix $H$ is Hermitian when $H^*=H$ and is positive semidefinite when $v^*Hv\ge0$ for every $v\in\mathbb C^3$, in the convention of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]](d), and $\langle g\rangle:=T^{-1}\int_0^Tg(t)\,dt$ with $T=2\pi/\omega$. The period-averaged work per unit volume, in $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-3}$, is

$$\langle E\cdot\partial_tP\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}(e^*\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)e).$$

It is nonnegative for every $e$ if and only if the full Hermitian dissipative part

$$M_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)=\frac{\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)-\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)^*}{2i}$$

is positive semidefinite. This frequencywise monochromatic passivity is an additional model condition, not a consequence of causality or dispersion.

For the instantaneous part set $S=(\chi_\infty+\chi_\infty^{\mathsf T})/2$ and $A=(\chi_\infty-\chi_\infty^{\mathsf T})/2$, so $S^{\mathsf T}=S$ and $A^{\mathsf T}=-A$. For any real $C^1$ history its exact instantaneous work split is

$$E\cdot\partial_t(\varepsilon_0\chi_\infty E)=\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}E\cdot S E\right)+\varepsilon_0 E\cdot A\partial_tE.$$

The symmetric part therefore supplies the quadratic storage term; no positivity of that term is asserted unless $S$ is additionally positive semidefinite. The antisymmetric part has $E\cdot A E=0$ but can supply nonzero work over a cycle. Its monochromatic contribution is $\varepsilon_0\omega\operatorname{Im}(e^*A e)/2$, and

$$M_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)=M_K(\omega)+A/i,\qquad M_K(\omega)=\frac{\chi(\omega)-\chi(\omega)^*}{2i}.$$

Thus only a symmetric real instantaneous matrix contributes purely this storage term for all histories; for an arbitrary real instantaneous matrix the passivity test must include its antisymmetric contribution. For example, $\chi_\infty=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\-1&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $K=0$ and $e=(1,i,0)^{\mathsf T}$ give $E=(\cos\omega t,\sin\omega t,0)$, zero quadratic storage and averaged work $\varepsilon_0\omega>0$. The opposite circular amplitude $(1,-i,0)^{\mathsf T}$ gives averaged work $-\varepsilon_0\omega$, so this instantaneous response is causal but fails the all-amplitude passivity condition.

**(e) [Scope]** The response is declared in the material rest frame of [[post-em-material-closure]](a); boosting the material changes the fields and the rest observer, and no frame-independent instantaneous response law is asserted. The framework does not claim that any particular material realises these branches, no microscopic mechanism is derived, and no empirical statement is made.

Assume the setting and hypotheses of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]] and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as carried by its suppliers: $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $a>0$, $t_0<T$, jointly $C^\infty$ fields $\rho,J$ vanishing outside $\overline B_a(0)\times[t_0,T]$ and satisfying $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$; let $\varphi,A$ be the retarded potentials and $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$, $B:=\nabla\times A$ the fields, with $S:=E\times B/\mu_0$ ([[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]], [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]]). Adopt the causal selection [[post-em-radiation-selection]]: these retarded fields are the fields of the source model (the compact smooth instance established by [[pthm-em-retarded-potentials]]). Define the **time-dependent electric dipole moment**

$$p(u):=\int_{B_a}y\,\rho(y,u)\,dy\in\mathbb R^3$$

(componentwise, about the fixed chart origin of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]; it is the fixed-time analogue of the static source moment of [[def-em-electric-moments]]), and, as in the asymptotic theorem, $I(n,u):=\int_{B_a}J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy$, $V(n,u):=\partial_uI(n,u)=\int_{B_a}J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy$ and

$$D(u):=\frac{a}{c}\int_{B_a}\sup_{|v-u|\le a/c}|J_{tt}(y,v)|\,dy.$$

Then:

(a) [Moment identities] $p\in C^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^3)$, $p'(u)=\int_{B_a}J(y,u)\,dy$, $p''(u)=\int_{B_a}J_t(y,u)\,dy$, $\int_{B_a}\rho_t(y,u)\,dy=0$ and the total charge $\int_{B_a}\rho(y,u)\,dy$ vanishes for every $u$.

(b) [Dipole replacement error] $|V(n,u)-p''(u)|\le D(u)$ for every $n\in S^2$ and every $u\in[t_0,T]$: the explicit absolute error of the dipole approximation to the source's transverse current moment.

(c) [Leading fields] With $\Gamma_E$, $\Gamma_B$ the constants of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]](b) (depending only on $a,c,\mu_0$ and the listed source suprema), for every $n\in S^2$, $u\in[t_0,T]$, $r\ge2a$:

$$\Bigl|E\bigl(rn,u+\tfrac rc\bigr)-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times p''(u))\Bigr|\le\frac{\Gamma_E}{r^2}+\frac{\mu_0D(u)}{4\pi r},\qquad \Bigl|B\bigl(rn,u+\tfrac rc\bigr)-\frac{n\times E(rn,u+\tfrac rc)}{c}\Bigr|\le\frac{\Gamma_B+\Gamma_E/c}{r^2}.$$

The displayed dipole field approximates the actual leading far field $E_{\rm lead}=\mu_0n\times(n\times V)/(4\pi r)$ with the stated absolute $D(u)/r$ error. Equality of these leading fields requires $n\times(n\times(V-p''))=0$; $V=p''$ and, in particular, $D(u)=0$ are sufficient. All errors are uniform in $n$ at fixed $u$.

(d) [Retarded-time radiated power] The limit of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]](c) equals $\mu_0|p''(u)|^2/(6\pi c)+R(u)$ with the explicit absolute error

$$|R(u)|\le\frac{\mu_0\bigl(2|p''(u)|D(u)+D(u)^2\bigr)}{4\pi c},\qquad\text{so}\qquad \lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S^2}r^2n\cdot S\bigl(rn,u+\tfrac rc\bigr)d\sigma=\frac{\mu_0}{6\pi c}|p''(u)|^2\ \text{ whenever } D(u)=0.$$

The evaluation uses the sphere moment $\int_{S^2}|n\times p''|^2d\sigma=(8\pi/3)|p''|^2$ of [[lem-em-sphere-zonal-moments]](d). The limit is at fixed retarded time $u$, not at fixed observation time.

(e) [Scope] The compact smooth source branch only; the dipole error is absolute and explicitly controlled by $D(u)$, and no assertion is made that slow or 'nonrelativistic' source motion alone makes $D(u)$ small -- that is a hypothesis on the source's time variation. No point charge, no moving point source, no radiation reaction, no self-force and no empirical or measurement content; the failure of the correspondence with an oscillator for rapidly varying sources is retained through $D(u)$. Separately retain the sharper actual source estimate $|B(rn,u+r/c)-n\times E_{\rm lead}(n,u,r)/c|\le\Gamma_B/r^2$, with $E_{\rm lead}=\mu_0n\times(n\times V)/(4\pi r)$; the bound against the actual E uses the combined constant displayed in (c).

Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with a chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$ ([[def-em-surface-distribution]]), let $\sigma_f:S\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $K_f:S\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous with $K_f(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ for all $(x,t)$ (a free surface charge density in $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-2}$ and a tangential free surface current density in $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, both stationary in $t$), and let $\rho_v:(\Omega\setminus S)\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $J_v:(\Omega\setminus S)\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous and locally integrable on $\Omega\times I$. Let $E,B,D,H:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be locally integrable on $\Omega\times I$ and of class $C^1$ on $(\Omega\setminus S)\times I$, with the joint one-sided $C^1$ extension property: around every $(x_0,t_0)\in S\times I$, each side of each field is the restriction of a $C^1$ function on an open spacetime neighbourhood of the corresponding closed side of a smaller stationary graph cylinder, so that the fields and their first space and time derivatives extend continuously to that side, locally uniformly on compact cylinders. Write $[F]=F_+-F_-$ for the jump of the one-sided traces.

**[Thin-interface hypothesis]** Suppose that $E,B,D,H$ satisfy the four macroscopic equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] in the distributional sense on $U$ with the source pair $\rho_f=\rho_v+\sigma_f\delta_S$, $J_f=J_v+K_f\delta_S$, where the stationary-sheet pairings are those of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c) and the equations are $\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD$ as identities in the sense of [[def-distribution]], the fields being identified with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $\psi$ ranging over $C_c^\infty(U)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]). This thin-interface solution hypothesis is a modelling assumption of the statement: it is the natural weakening of the smooth macroscopic equations to fields with a common stationary discontinuity, and it is not deduced from the smooth-region equations alone.

Then, pointwise on $S\times I$,

$$n\cdot[D]=\sigma_f,\qquad n\cdot[B]=0,\qquad n\times[E]=0,\qquad n\times[H]=K_f,$$

with the Euclidean inner and cross products of the one-sided traces ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]); equivalently $\sigma_f=n\cdot[D]$ and $K_f=n\times[H]$ recover the free sheet densities from the field jumps.

Merely having one-sided spatial $C^1$ traces separately at every time does not justify the last upgrade.

**[Scope]** In the joint one-sided spacetime $C^1$ extension branch, stationarity and the joint extensions make $\partial_tD$ and $\partial_tB$ locally bounded near $S$ and hence locally integrable, contributing no delta terms. In the weak-trace branch the explicitly assumed locally integrable temporal derivatives provide this conclusion instead. No magnetic charge and no magnetic surface current are present in the sources; no dipolar sheet layer (a concentrated dipole distribution in $P$ or $M$, which would make the fields non-integrable) is included. No existence theorem for fields with singular sources is asserted, no constitutive law is used, and no empirical claim is made.

Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ and $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, and let
$(E,B)$ be the plane-wave fields of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on the
whole-space region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, with the terminology and
phase convention of that definition, the cross product and inner product of
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] extended to
$\mathbb C^3$ componentwise, the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and
$\hat k=k/|k|$. Then:

(a) [Amplitude equations] $(E,B)$ satisfies the four smooth-branch vacuum
Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with $\rho\equiv0$ and
$J\equiv0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if

$$k\cdot e=0,\qquad k\cdot b=0,\qquad k\times e=\omega b,\qquad k\times b=-\frac{\omega}{c^2}e .$$

(b) [Dispersion, nonzero waves, two polarizations] The amplitude equations
admit a nonzero solution $(e,b)\ne(0,0)$ if and only if
$|k|^2=\omega^2/c^2$; off this dispersion relation the only solution is
$e=b=0$. On the dispersion relation both zero and nonzero solutions occur; a
particular solution is nonzero exactly when its amplitudes are not both zero,
in the sense of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]](c). If $|k|=\omega/c$, the
solutions are exactly the pairs $(e,b)$ with
$e\in\{v\in\mathbb C^3: k\cdot v=0\}$ arbitrary and $b=k\times e/\omega$: a
complex two-dimensional family; $e=0$ gives the zero wave, and for every
nonzero solution $e\ne0$ and $b\ne0$.

(c) [Transversality, orthogonality, magnitude relation and the wave equation]
For every solution with $|k|=\omega/c$ and every
$(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: $k\cdot E(x,t)=k\cdot B(x,t)=0$,
$E(x,t)\cdot B(x,t)=0$ and $B(x,t)=\hat k\times E(x,t)/c$; in particular
$|B(x,t)|=|E(x,t)|/c$. Each component of $E$ and of $B$ is a $C^\infty$
solution of the wave equation $\Delta v=c^{-2}\partial_t^2v$ of
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]] on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$.

(d) [Scope] The equivalence in (a) is between the amplitude equations and
membership in the source-free smooth Maxwell branch; it says nothing about
fields that solve the wave equations but not the amplitude equations (see
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]](b)). The item covers ideal whole-space plane
waves only, makes no finite-energy, boundary, material or empirical claim, and
is conditional on the adopted postulate.

$$U_q(\delta,R):=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\{\delta\le|x-x_0|\le R\}}|E_q(x)|^2\,d\lambda_3(x)$$

Let the laboratory region, chart and units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], so that $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $W:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ is the wave expression of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]. Let $a>0$, $t_0<T$ and let $\rho:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $J:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be source fields of [[def-em-sources]] that are jointly of class $C^\infty$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], vanish identically outside the compact set $\overline B_a(0)\times[t_0,T]$, and satisfy the continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ everywhere --- the compatibility condition that [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] shows to be forced by the Maxwell system, here assumed for the prescribed source. Define the retarded potentials by the explicit retarded integrals

$$\varphi(x,t):=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\rho\bigl(y,t-|x-y|/c\bigr)}{|x-y|}\,dy,\qquad A(x,t):=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{J\bigl(y,t-|x-y|/c\bigr)}{|x-y|}\,dy,$$

and put $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$, $B:=\nabla\times A$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]], [[def-em-fields]]). Then:

(a) [Smoothness and wave equations] $\varphi$ and each component of $A$ are of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, and $W\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $WA=\mu_0J$ pointwise.

(b) [Lorenz gauge] With $G:=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$ one has $G=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: the retarded pair is in Lorenz gauge, the continuity hypothesis supplies this identity and the total-charge conclusion (f).

(c) [Maxwell fields] $E$ and $B$ are of class $C^\infty$ and the tuple $(E,B,\rho,J)$ satisfies the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the whole of $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\nabla\times E=-\partial_tB$, $\nabla\times B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$.

(d) [No field before the source] $E=B=0$ at every event with $t<t_0$ (indeed $\varphi=A=0$ there): the selected retarded solution carries no field from before the source acted.

(e) [Zero-data Cauchy identification] For every $t_1<t_0$ the pair $(\varphi,A)$ restricted to $\mathbb R^3\times[t_1,\infty)$ is the unique $C^2$ extension solution of the wave Cauchy problem of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] at time $t_1$ with zero Cauchy data and sources $\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\mu_0J$.

(f) [Total charge] The total charge $Q(t):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho(y,t)\,dy$ is zero for every $t$: a source that is smooth, compactly supported in space and restricted to a compact time interval and satisfies continuity carries zero total charge, so this branch does not model an eternal isolated nonzero charge.

(g) [Scope] This is the compact smooth branch with an adopted causal selection; it asserts nothing about point, line or sheet sources, about weak or distributional branches, about finite-energy or decay properties, about radiation reaction or self-force, and no empirical claim. In particular the fields of a prescribed isolated point charge with an eternal worldline are not covered by this theorem and are supplied separately by the point-source items of this page.

## Remarks

Every cited conditional result retains its stated hypotheses. In particular, the point-source and causal-wave comparisons below assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) through their source suppliers; this qualification supplies no additional field or self-interaction model.

Record, with no speculative content, the limits of the radiation model built on this page.

(a) [Self-energy] For nonzero charge $q\ne0$, the truncated electrostatic field energy of the stationary idealized point charge diverges as the inner cutoff is removed ([[pthm-em-point-self-energy-divergence]]): the point source's own field carries infinite energy in this framework's idealization, and any finite-energy treatment of a point-like charge requires modifying the source or the field near the singularity, or an explicit cutoff, none of which is supplied here. The $q=0$ branch has zero field energy and no divergence.

(b) [Undefined self-interaction; nonzero and zero source branches] The framework's source model [[def-em-weak-sources]] pairs distributions against compact smooth tests and expressly excludes arbitrary products of distributions. An explicit nonzero singular self-field is the stationary Coulomb field of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](d): for a constant trajectory $z(t)=x_0$ and $q\ne0$, $|E_q(x)|=|q|/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-x_0|^2)$ for $x\ne x_0$, which tends to infinity as $x\to x_0$. Its point-source charge distribution is supported on that stationary worldline. For $q=0$, the point-source pairings of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) give $\rho_{\mathrm{pt}}=J_{\mathrm{pt}}=0$ for every admitted trajectory; in the stationary Coulomb source-field branch, $E_q=0$ off $x_0$ extends smoothly by zero, with $B=0$. Thus that zero-source branch has no self-field singularity and no nontrivial self-interaction. This states the source-field branch, not uniqueness among fields with an additional free field.

The moving pure point-source branch retains a precise general obstruction: if $q\ne0$, $z$ is an admitted $C^1$ proper trajectory, and locally integrable fields satisfy the distributional Maxwell equations with exactly its point-source pair ([[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]], [[def-em-weak-sources]](b),(e)), there is no $C^1$ extension of the electric field through any interior worldline event that still satisfies those sourced equations. To see this, suppose such an extension exists near $(x_0,t_0)=(z(t_0),t_0)$ and write $g=\operatorname{div}E$. Its distributional divergence is the regular distribution of this continuous $g$ by [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]], under the stated Countable Choice convention. On a fixed compact box inside that neighbourhood, $|g|\le M<\infty$ by [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]. Choose a spatial bump $0\le\phi_r\le1$, equal to one on $B_{r/2}(x_0)$ and supported in $B_r(x_0)$; continuity of $z$ gives a time interval $J_r$ about $t_0$, inside that fixed box's time interval, with $z(J_r)\subset B_{r/2}(x_0)$. Choose a nonzero nonnegative smooth temporal bump $\eta_r$ supported in $J_r$, with $A_r=\int\eta_r\,dt>0$ ([[lem-scaled-euclidean-bumps-with-compact-support-and-gradient-bound]]). The compact smooth test $\phi_r(x)\eta_r(t)$ has charge pairing $qA_r$, whereas its pairing with $g$ has modulus at most $M(2r)^3A_r$: the spatial support lies in the side-$2r$ cube, and iterated integration of the continuous compactly supported integrand gives this bound ([[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]], [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]], [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]]). The sourced Gauss identity would therefore give $|q|/\varepsilon_0\le M(2r)^3$ for every sufficiently small $r>0$, an impossibility. This is a failure of a $C^1$ sourced extension, not a claim that every moving field norm blows up; the explicit norm blowup above is the stationary Coulomb case.

For nonzero singular self-fields, evaluating the field on its own point-source support or forming its product with the distributional source is not supplied by these postulates. A vanishing component of the current does not remedy the singular charge-field product. More generally the prescribed moving-source framework supplies no arbitrary distribution-product operation, regularization or self-force equation; its emitted-power results below do not introduce one. No moving-source norm blowup is inferred from the stationary example, and no equation of motion is derived in either charge branch.

(c) [What the emitted-power items do and do not give] [[pthm-em-larmor-nonrelativistic]] and [[pthm-em-lienard-emitted-power]] are prescribed-source statements: they compute the emitted power of a stipulated worldline at a stipulated emission event, per unit laboratory emission time, using the retarded-time conversion factor in their weighted far-zone flux definition. At an instantaneous-rest emission event that factor is one, so the power also equals the fixed-sphere flux specified in [[pthm-em-larmor-nonrelativistic]](e). These results determine no worldline evolution, no back-reaction and no mechanical energy-loss rate of the particle; identifying the emitted power with such a loss rate requires an additional mechanical balance assumption.

(d) [Deferred, not claimed] Extended-charge or finite-size regularizations of the self-field, the well-posedness of any self-force dynamics, runaway solutions and an electromagnetic derivation of rest mass are outside this page and are neither stated nor proved here. No experiment, measurement, statistical estimate or precision is reported or implied, and nothing in this remark is a refutation of any physical theory.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded contractible Lipschitz polyhedron and let $\{\mathcal T_h\}$ be a shape-regular family of matching affine tetrahedral meshes with $h=\max_K\operatorname{diam}K\to0$. Set $V_h=N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ and $S_h=W_h^0\cap H_0^1(\Omega)$, and define
$$X_h=\{v_h\in V_h:(v_h,\nabla q_h)_{L^2}=0\text{ for every }q_h\in S_h\}.$$
Every sequence $v_h\in X_h$ bounded in $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ has a subsequence converging strongly in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$. Moreover there is $C$ independent of $h$ such that $\|v_h\|_2\le C\|\operatorname{curl}v_h\|_2$ for all $v_h\in X_h$.

The precise harmonic-quotient version is as follows. On any bounded Lipschitz polyhedron for which the regular decomposition and relative commuting projections below are proved, put $K=\ker(\operatorname{curl}|_{H_0(\operatorname{curl})})$, $K_h=\ker(\operatorname{curl}|_{V_h})$ and
$$\mathcal H=K\cap(\nabla H_0^1)^\perp,\qquad\mathcal H_h=K_h\cap(\nabla S_h)^\perp.$$
Both harmonic spaces are finite dimensional. Discrete compactness still holds on $X_h$, while the uniform curl Poincare inequality holds on $Z_h=V_h\cap K_h^\perp=X_h\cap\mathcal H_h^\perp$. A nonzero vector of $\mathcal H_h$ prevents that inequality on all of $X_h$. These are the harmonic spaces of the relative boundary complex; the full-space absolute cohomology dimensions do not identify them.

Assume Countable Choice for the H(curl), H(div), and real $L^2$ inner-product interfaces used here; no full Axiom of Choice is assumed.
